title: 3  Background
text:
3.1 What is Open Science?
Open Science (or Open Research) is an approach to conducting and communicating research that aims to make all stages of the research process more transparent, accessible, reproducible, and collaborative. It extends beyond open access publishing to encompass the sharing of data, software, methods, materials, peer review, and other research outputs throughout the research lifecycle (Hardwicke & Vazire, 2024). Together, these practices help build trust, accelerate progress, promote equity, and strengthen the research community.

title: 3  Background
text:
Note“Open Science” and “Open Research”?



The terms Open Science and Open Research are often used interchangeably. Open Science has become the internationally recognised term adopted by organisations such as UNESCO and the European Commission to describe a broad movement towards greater transparency, accessibility, collaboration, and reproducibility throughout the research process. Despite its name, UNESCO explicitly defines Open Science as encompassing the natural sciences, social sciences, humanities, and the arts (UNESCO, 2021). Nevertheless, many scholars, particularly in the humanities, prefer the term Open Research, arguing that it more naturally reflects the diversity of scholarly traditions beyond the sciences (Adams et al., 2026). Throughout this repository, we use Open Research when referring to research practices across the full spectrum of music research, while recognising Open Science as the broader international framework within which these practices have developed.

title: 3  Background
text:
3.2 Why Open Research?
Open research serves several complementary purposes. At its foundation, it fosters trust by making research transparent, allowing others to scrutinise, verify, and reproduce scientific claims. Building on this, openness enables progress by transforming publications, data, code, and methods into reusable resources that accelerate cumulative discovery rather than requiring each project to start from scratch. Finally, open research supports community by supporting learning, collaboration, and engagement both within academia and beyond. This reveals the often hidden processes of scientific inquiry, enabling students and researchers to learn not only from published results but also from the decisions, workflows, and materials that produced them. Together, these three levels (trust, progress, and community) capture the broader value of open research as a foundation for more reliable, cumulative, and accessible science.



Three levels of open research - trust for producing reliable knowledge, progress for advancing and supporting cumulative collective knowledge, and community to support learning and and collaboration.



3.2.1 Trust
Research advances through trust – but not blind trust. Confidence in research findings is earned when claims can be inspected, questioned, and independently verified. Open research attempts to shift the basis of trust from the reputation of individual researchers to the transparency of the scientific process itself. Publications, data, analysis scripts, study materials, preregistrations, and peer review provide the evidence needed for others to evaluate, reproduce, and extend previous work (Nosek et al., 2015).
This need is particularly pressing in music research, where studies often involve complex combinations of musical stimuli, behavioural or physiological measurements, computational analyses, and subjective interpretations. In music psychology, trust depends on knowing precisely which stimuli were used, how participants were recruited, how emotional or cognitive responses were measured, and how analyses were conducted. In music information retrieval (MIR) and computational musicology, reproducibility requires access to datasets, feature extraction pipelines, machine learning models, software versions, and evaluation procedures. Digital humanities projects frequently involve intricate data transformations, annotation decisions, and computational workflows that are impossible to fully describe within the constraints of a journal article. Even in historical musicology, where primary sources are often publicly available, transparency about editorial choices, coding decisions, and analytical procedures strengthens confidence in scholarly interpretations.
Open research makes these otherwise hidden aspects of research visible. Sharing data, code, materials, and complete analytical workflows allows others to verify findings, identify errors, assess methodological choices, and reproduce results. Transparency also discourages questionable research practices by making research decisions more explicit and accountable. Importantly, openness does not guarantee that research is correct; rather, it allows the research community to evaluate the strength of the evidence and to improve upon it over time.
Despite broad recognition of these benefits, adoption remains uneven. Within music psychology, for example, journal policies increasingly encourage researchers to share data and analysis scripts, yet voluntary encouragement alone has resulted in relatively limited uptake as a sample of studies in music psychology indicates that about 5% studies share data and 1% share analysis scripts (Eerola, 2024). Building a more trustworthy discipline therefore requires moving beyond encouragement towards research practices in which openness becomes the expected default rather than the exception.
Practices that contribute to trust include open access publications, open data, open-source code, reproducible analytical workflows, replication studies, preregistration, Registered Reports, and, where appropriate, open peer review. Together, these practices make scientific claims inspectable rather than merely believable.


3.2.2 Progress
Research should not merely produce knowledge; it should enable future knowledge. Open research transforms publications, datasets, software, and analytical workflows into resources that others can reuse, extend, and improve (Lowndes et al., 2017). Rather than requiring every research group to rebuild datasets and methods from scratch, openness enables cumulative science. Data can be reused, software extended, methods refined, and findings independently replicated, allowing scientific knowledge to develop more efficiently.
These benefits are particularly important in music research. The creation of musical corpora is often resource intensive, involving recording, transcription, annotation, or specialist cultural knowledge (Hentschel et al., 2025). Behavioural ratings and expert annotations likewise require substantial effort and can support benchmarking, secondary analyses, and computational modelling when they are shared.
Progress also depends on transparent methods. Research in music psychology, music information retrieval, computational musicology, and the digital humanities frequently relies on complex computational pipelines that cannot be fully described in a journal article. Sharing code, software versions, and documentation allows others to reproduce, adapt, and extend these workflows. Open-source software also remains useful for longer when it is version-controlled, archived, and maintained by a wider community.
Finally, sharing alone is not enough. For research outputs to support cumulative science, they must be well documented and reusable. The FAIR principles—making data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable—highlight the importance of metadata, persistent repositories, clear licensing, and standardised formats that allow publications, datasets, code, and other research outputs to remain useful long after the original study has been completed (Wilkinson et al., 2016).
Practices that support progress include FAIR data, shared datasets, reusable software, replication studies, standardised metadata, persistent repositories, version control, and reproducible computational environments. Together, these practices transform individual research projects into lasting resources for collaboration, innovation, and cumulative scientific progress.


3.2.3 Community
Open research is fundamentally a community practice. Science advances not only through new discoveries but also through the exchange of knowledge, skills, methods, and resources that enable others to contribute. By making publications, data, code, workflows, and reviews openly available, researchers create opportunities for collaboration, mutual learning, and collective improvement. Open repositories reveal many aspects of research that are normally hidden from the published article, making the scientific process itself a shared community resource.
This community-building role extends across all areas of open science (Allen & Mehler, 2019). Open access publications broaden participation in scholarship; open data and code enable researchers to verify findings, develop new analyses, and acquire practical skills; reproducible workflows provide examples of good research practice; preregistrations and Registered Reports demonstrate transparent study design; open peer review exposes the constructive dialogue that improves research; and replication studies reinforce the collective responsibility of maintaining a reliable scientific record.
Open science also fosters communities that extend beyond individual projects and institutions. Researchers benefit not only from shared resources but also from networks that exchange expertise, develop standards, and promote best practices (McKiernan et al., 2016). Communities such as ReproducibiliTea, The Turing Way, and discipline-specific open science initiatives provide training materials, discussion forums, workshops, mentoring, and collaborative support that help embed openness into everyday research practice.
Finally, openness increases the reach of music research beyond academia. Teachers, musicians, software developers, cultural organisations, policy makers, journalists, and interested members of the public can all benefit from unrestricted access to publications, data, educational resources, and software. By lowering barriers to participation, open research strengthens connections between researchers and the wider society, increasing both the visibility and the impact of music research.


3.2.4 Equity
Open research promotes a more equitable scientific ecosystem by reducing barriers to accessing and contributing to knowledge (UNESCO, 2021). The ability to read scientific publications, use research data, or apply analytical methods should not depend on the financial resources of an institution or the country in which a researcher works. Open Access publications, openly shared datasets, software, and educational resources help level the playing field by making high-quality research available to anyone with an internet connection.
Greater equity also broadens participation in science. Researchers in low-resource settings, independent scholars, students, practitioners, and citizen scientists can contribute more fully when knowledge and research tools are openly available. In music research, this is particularly important for supporting underrepresented musical traditions, fostering international collaboration, and enabling a more diverse range of perspectives to shape the discipline. By democratising access to knowledge and research resources, open science helps create a more inclusive and globally connected research community. However, achieving equity through open science is not automatic feature of the scheme but requires careful implementation and how stakeholders value and provide support for it (Bezuidenhout, 2025).

title: 4  Availability of publications
text:
4.1 Open publications
There are several routes for making publications openly available, each with different cost structures, embargo conditions, and implications for funder compliance. For a concise overview of Open Access (OA) publishing, see Suber (2012).

title: 4  Availability of publications
text:
Gold OA: Publishing in a fully open-access journal where all content is immediately and permanently free to read without restrictions. Authors usually pay an Article Processing Charge (APC), through this varies widely by journal and discipline.
Hybrid OA: A subscription journal that allows individual articles to be made open access for a fee. Some funder mandates (e.g., Plan S, UKRI, NIH) increasingly require immediate public access to accepted manuscripts, with no embargo under updated policies, which limits how straightforward hybrid options are. Under plan S in particular, hybrid journals are generally only compliant when covered by transformative agreements or formal transition pathways.
Diamond / Platinum OA: Journals that are fully open access with no charges for authors or readers. These are typically supported by universities, societies, or library consortia. Several music journals follow this model (see below). For a broader overview, see Bosman et al. (2021).
Green OA (self-archiving): Depositing the accepted manuscript in a repository such as Zenodo, arXiv (see below), or an institutional repository. Policies differ by publisher, especially around embargo length and which versions can be shared: Jisc - Open policy finder can be used for checking journal-specific policies. In the EU, Horizon Europe encourages this route and expects immediate open access to accepted manuscrits via repositories.
APC costs and waivers: APCs range from a few hundred to several thousand USD or EUR. Some publishers offer waivers or discounts for researchers without funding or from low-income countries, so it is worth checking before assuming APC-based OA is not feasible.

title: 4  Availability of publications
text:
4.2 OA publishing in numbers
Open access publishing has grown substantially over the past decade, though the landscape remains uneven. Between 2014 and 2024, the share of global scholarly articles made available via gold OA rose from 14% to 40%, while the subscription-only share fell from 70% to 54% (STM Association, 2024). This shift has been driven in part by funder mandates, but also by the rapid growth of APC-funded publishing, which carries its own equity concerns: annual global APC spending across six major publishers alone almost tripled from $910 million in 2019 to $2.5 billion in 2023 (Haustein et al., 2024).
These figures describe the overall scholarly publishing market. Music research sits within this landscape but has its own characteristics: a mix of humanities, social science, and engineering publication norms; a strong conference culture in MIR; and a notable cluster of diamond OA journals (TISMIR, EMR) that charge neither authors nor readers. title: 4  Availability of publications
text:
4.3 Preprints
Preprints, i.e., versions of manuscripts shared publicly before or alongside formal peer review, are now a widely used mechanism for rapid and open dissemination. For practical guidance on posting and managing preprints across the publication pipeline, see Moshontz et al. (2021).

Where to post (varies by subdiscipline):

arXiv (categories cs.SD and eess.AS) for Music Information Retrieval (MIR), music technology, and Machine Leanring(ML)-adjacent work

PsyArXiv for music psychology

OSF Preprints for interdisciplinary work

Zenodo for general-purpose dissemination, including datasets and code alongside papers

SSRN for social science and related interdisciplinary work

HAL for computer science, engineering, humanities, and social sciences

Subdiscipline norms vary widely: Preprinting is well established in MIR and ML-adjacent music research, where posting on arXiv prior to or alongside ISMIR, ICASSP, or NeurIPS submissions is standard practice. Uptake is still uneven in music psychology and remains limited in musicology and music education, although adoption is gradually increasing.
Versioning: When a preprint is later published, the two versions should be explicitly linked (for example via DOI cross-references). Some repositories, such as PsyArXiv, support metadata linking that helps citation systems merge records across versions.
Journal prior-posting policies: Most journals now allow preprints, but conditions still vary regarding timing, licensing, and accepted manuscript versions. It is advisable to verify specific policies via Jisc - Open policy finder before submission.
Citation advantage of preprints: Several large-scale studies report that papers with an associated preprint tend to receive earlier and often higher citation counts compared to those without preprints, likely due to earlier visibility and dissemination (e.g., Serghiou & Ioannidis (2018), Fraser et al. (2020)).
Academic sharing platforms: Services such as ResearchGate and Academia.edu are often used to upload and circulate papers, including preprints. However, they are not formal preprint repositories and do not provide consistent long-term preservation or clear policy compliance guarantees. They function more as academic networking and sharing spaces than as archival infrastructure.
Secondary interpretation tools: Services such as arXivExplained and similar paper summarisation tools sit one step removed from publication. They help make preprints easier to read and explore, but they are not repositories and do not host canonical versions of research outputs. They are interpretation layers rather than publication infrastructure.

4.4 Journal and conference landscape by subdiscipline
The following list of representative journals and major venues is not exhaustive. In addition, OA status and APC policies can change, so verify on the journal’s website before submitting.
Music psychology

Music Perception — subscription (UC Press), hybrid OA option available
Music & Science — fully OA (SAGE), APC applies (waivers available)
Psychomusicology: Music, Mind, and Brain — subscription (APA), hybrid OA option
Empirical Musicology Review — fully OA, no APC; diamond model, published by The Ohio State University Libraries
Frontiers in Psychology (Auditory Cognitive Neuroscience section) — fully OA, APC applies; used widely for music perception and cognition work

Computational musicology / MIR

Transactions of the International Society for Music Information Retrieval (TISMIR) — fully OA, no APC; diamond model and the flagship journal of the MIR community; also actively encourages open data and code archiving alongside submissions
Journal of New Music Research — subscription (Taylor & Francis), hybrid OA option
Computer Music Journal — subscription (MIT Press), hybrid OA option
ACM Transactions on Multimedia Computing, Communications, and Applications (TOMM) — subscription with OA option; covers music retrieval and multimedia processing
IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing (TASLP) — subscription with OA option; a principal journal for audio/music ML methods

Musicology
Musicology journals are typically published by societies (i.e., American Musicological Society, Royal Musical Association, Society for Music Analysis) or major humanities presses (Oxford, Cambridge, Chicago). Fully OA options are limited; Green OA via author self-archiving is often the most realistic route. OA monograph publishing is underdeveloped in this space, which matters because the monograph is a primary output form in musicology.
Music education
Music education journals span a range of publishers and have uneven OA uptake. The Journal of Research in Music Education and Music Education Research both offer hybrid OA options.
Cross-disciplinary / psychology-adjacent

Collabra: Psychology — fully OA, APC applies but with a liberal waiver policy; suitable for music psychology work following open science practices

AI and music technology conferences
Much of the most impactful more technical music AI research is (first) published at conferences, not journals. The OA status varies by venue:

ISMIR — fully OA proceedings; the primary venue for MIR and computational music research
ICASSP (IEEE) — IEEE Xplore, subscription access; widely used for audio and music signal processing
NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR — open proceedings; music-adjacent work on generative models, audio representations, and music understanding appears here with increasing frequency
AAAI — open proceedings on AAAI Digital Library; has received music-related submissions across generation, recommendation, and analysis
NIME (New Interfaces for Musical Expression) — open proceedings; relevant for music technology and creative practice
SMC (Sound and Music Computing) — open proceedings; bridges signal processing, AI, and musicology

A note on conference vs. journal culture: in MIR and music AI, conference papers at ISMIR, ICASSP, NeurIPS, and related venues carry significant weight and are treated as primary research contributions, in contrast to humanities norms where journal articles and monographs are expected.

title: 4  Availability of publications
text:
4.5 Metrics, rankings, and research evaluation
When selecting a publication venue, it is important to consider how research outputs are evaluated varies across the subdisciplines in music research. This is particularly important for early-career researchers or those moving between institutions.

4.5.1 Journal impact factors and DORA
The Journal Impact Factor (IF) is a journal-level metric measuring average citations per article over a two-year window. Despite its widespread use in hiring, promotion, and grant decisions, it has well-documented limitations: citation distributions within journals are highly skewed, the metric is field-specific and cannot be compared across disciplines, and it can be gamed through editorial policy (Cell Biology et al., 2012). The San Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA), now signed by hundreds of funders and institutions worldwide, calls explicitly for research to be assessed on its own merits rather than on the basis of the journal in which it is published (Cell Biology et al., 2012). The Leiden Manifesto (Hicks et al., 2015) and the Responsible Metrics framework extend these principles to bibliometrics more broadly.
For music researchers, IF is often irrelevant or misleading: many leading music journals have no IF (TISMIR, EMR), musicology journals have structurally low citation rates compared to STEM journals, and much MIR research is published at conferences that have no IF at all. Researchers should be cautious about using IF to compare venues across these subdisciplines.
An important alternative is the Source Normalized Impact per Paper (SNIP), which adjusts for field-specific citation practices by weighting citations against the citation potential of each subject area. This makes it more suitable than the raw IF for comparing across the disciplinary mix found in music research Moed (2010).


4.5.2 Conference rankings (for MIR and music technology researchers)
In computer science (CS), conference papers carry primary publication weight. Several systems are used to rank conferences:

ICORE / CORE rankings (portal.core.edu.au): The standard CS conference ranking, using categories A* (flagship), A (excellent), B (good), C (basic). Managed by the Computing Research and Education Association of Australasia and now an international collaboration. Widely used in hiring and grant assessment in Australia, Singapore, and parts of Europe. ISMIR is not ranked in CORE; ICASSP is ranked B; NeurIPS, ICML, and ICLR are A*.
CSRankings (csrankings.org): A faculty-level metric ranking CS institutions by publications at a selective list of top venues. ISMIR is not included in CSRankings, which can disadvantage MIR researchers in CS departments where it is used for hiring benchmarking.
Qualis (Brazil) and ERA (Australia): Country-specific conference and journal ranking systems used in national research evaluation frameworks; the CORE ranking is now partially aligned with ERA.

A practical consequence: an MIR researcher publishing primarily at ISMIR and ICASSP may be medium-positioned under CORE and invisible in CSRankings, leading CS researchers to step beyond the music research community and target more general CS conferences that are higher ranked. Many of these, such as AAAI, have recently started `Music (or audio) tracks’.


4.5.3 Useful tools for finding metrics and rankings

Google Scholar — citation counts and h-index; also tracks preprints and grey literature
Semantic Scholar — AI-assisted citation graph, good for MIR/CS papers
OpenAlex — fully open bibliometric database; a DORA-compatible alternative to Web of Science and Scopus
Scimago Journal Rank (SJR) — journal rankings based on Scopus data; covers many music journals
ICORE portal — CORE conference rankings, searchable
Jisc Open Policy Finder — OA policy compliance checker (replaces Sherpa/RoMEO)



4.5.4 A note on the h-index across disciplines
The h-index is a researcher-level metric defined as the number h such that h papers have at least h citations each. It is used in some hiring and grant contexts as a proxy for research impact. However, h-index values are structurally incomparable across fields: a music psychologist and a computer vision researcher will accumulate citations at very different rates, and an interdisciplinary researcher publishing across musicology and MIR may be disadvantaged in both fields’ norms simultaneously. DORA and the Leiden Manifesto both caution against decontextualised use of h-index in research assessment.

title: 4  Availability of publications
text:
4.6 Authorship / Attribution of credit / ORCIDs
Authorship conventions and credit attribution differ across music research subdisciplines and can form a source of ambiguity, particularly in large or interdisciplinary collaborations. For an extensive discussion of author sequence and contribution in multiauthored publications, the reader is referred to Tscharntke et al. (2007).

Authorship criteria: Most publishers follow ICMJE-style guidelines requiring that authors have contributed substantially to conception, execution, or interpretation; drafted or critically revised the work; approved the final version; and agreed to be accountable for it. Note that being named in acknowledgements is not authorship.
CRediT (Contributor Roles Taxonomy): The CRediT taxonomy provides 14 standardised roles (Conceptualization, Data Curation, Formal Analysis, Funding Acquisition, Investigation, Methodology, Project Administration, Resources, Software, Supervision, Validation, Visualization, Writing (Original Draft, Writing), and Review & Editing) for explicitly attributing what each contributor did (Brand et al., 2015). This taxonomy is now supported by all major publishers and is an ANSI/NISO standard. CRediT does not determine who qualifies as an author; it makes the contributions transparent within the author list and beyond it.
ORCIDs: ORCID (Open Researcher and Contributor ID) is a persistent, unique digital identifier for researchers, free to register. It disambiguates authors across name changes, transliteration variants, or common surnames, and links research outputs, affiliations, and grants to a single record. Most major journals and funding agencies now require or strongly encourage ORCID registration at submission. Registering and maintaining an ORCID record is particularly important for early-career researchers whose publication record is still accumulating, and for researchers with names that are common or that vary across publications.
Disciplinary variation: Authorship norms differ across subdisciplines. In MIR and music technology, large multi-author collaborative papers (e.g., shared datasets, benchmarks, evaluation campaigns) are increasingly common and benefit most from CRediT transparency. In musicology, single- and dual-author papers remain the norm, and the concept of contributorship is less familiar. Music psychology sits closer to psychology norms, where author contribution statements are increasingly standard.
AI authorship: There is emerging consensus that generative AI tools (LLMs, etc.) cannot be listed as authors, as they cannot take responsibility for the work (Lund & Naheem, 2024). Their use should instead be disclosed in a methods or acknowledgements statement. Several major publishers (Elsevier, Springer Nature, PLOS) have adopted explicit policies to this effect.

title: 5  Open Data
text:
5.1 Why open data?
The operating principle for open data in research — as open as possible, as closed as necessary (UK Research and Innovation, 2016) — is simple to state but requires emphasis on both halves. Open should be the default position, and restricting access to data requires a specific justification (e.g., legal, ethical, commercial). The starting question for any music research project is not “should we share our data?” but “what, specifically, would prevent us from sharing, and does that actually apply here?”
Research data is the most valuable thing a study offers as the evidence that enables the paper’s written interpretation. When data is unavailable, findings cannot be verified, errors cannot be caught, questions not asked by the original study cannot be investigated or built upon by anyone else, and the investment of researcher time and participant effort remains locked inside a single publication. Opening up data is the way in which that investment pays forward — into meta-analyses, replication attempts, reuse in new contexts, and access for researchers who could not otherwise afford to collect equivalent material.

title: 5  Open Data
text:
5.2 But what counts as “data”?
Music research spans “traditional”/“hard” science disciplines, to the arts, humanities, and social sciences (AHSS) — all with different forms of data and varying relationships to openness.
MIR and computational musicology have stronger dataset-sharing cultures; experimental music psychology is moving towards openness but inherits norms from psychology where progress has been uneven (Eerola, 2024); and musicology, ethnomusicology, music education, and practice research operate within AHSS traditions where the nature of the data itself does not map cleanly onto the frameworks developed for quantitative science. The AHSS understanding of “data” is intentionally expansive as information used for reference and analysis (Gilby et al., 2022).

FAIR principles — Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable — addressed in Section 5.3, were developed primarily with computational and quantitative datasets in mind, stipulating technical principles for STEM-leaning data. C.O.R.E. data (Adams et al., 2026; Gilby et al., 2022), on the other hand, offers an adapted complementary (not competing) framework tailored for data from AHSS disciplines, where FAIR principles don’t necessarily translate or apply in the same ways. CORE speaks to the nature, context, and interpretive aspects of AHSS data types themselves and what openness means for them.






CORE describes research data as:

Collected — AHSS researchers typically gather, curate, and select from existing sources (e.g., texts, interviews, musical scores, recordings, images, objects, annotations, fieldwork notes, performances, archival materials), rather than necessarily generating their data. The collection and curation is itself a scholarly contribution, not merely a precursor to analysis.
Organised — the data has been structured, annotated, and made navigable. Organisational work is interpretive, so should be documented and shared.
Recontextualised — AHSS data typically does not exist independently of the scholarly conversation it enters. Sharing data means sharing the interpretive context that makes it meaningful and the disciplinary debates it speaks to, furthering cultural conversations about discoveries, methods, and debates.
Explained — transparency about how the data was worked with, coded, and interpreted is part of the analytical process and is itself a form of data sharing, even when the raw material cannot be released.




AHSS offers a broader understanding of shareable outputs for all music researchers beyond what most “traditional” open science frameworks capture. Alongside standard open science outputs (methodology, code, results, publications, preregistrations, preprints, open peer review), AHSS researchers can share research practice reflections, audio-visual materials, protocols, discussion documentation, annotated bibliographies, and researcher notes. These contributions should be understood as legitimate and valuable to open research in their own right, not merely a fallback option for the ethical impossibility (or personal unwillingness) of sharing raw data (Adams et al., 2026; Gilby et al., 2022).
Contrary to standard understandings of reproducibility and interoperability applicable to STEM open data, AHSS open data are better understood as material to be built upon and modified through further recontextualisation rather than simply reproduced. Sharing CORE data means sharing the conditions of its production, history, limits, and its relationships to data in other forms — manuscripts, printed scores, recordings, performances.
For current open practices in music psychology, see Eerola (2024). For computational musicology and MIR, see Moss & Neuwirth (2021). For a broader account of openness in AHSS research beyond STEM, see Adams et al. (2026) and Gilby et al. (2022).

title: 5  Open Data
section: 5.4 “As open as possible, as closed as necessary”
text:
5.4 “As open as possible, as closed as necessary”
The principle as open as possible, as closed as necessary (UK Research and Innovation, 2016) was designed with qualitative and sensitive data in mind as much as quantitative datasets. It is not a formula for excusing restricted access, but a requirement that restrictions be justified by specific constraints (e.g., ethical, legal, commercial). For much qualitative and AHSS research — interviews, ethnographic fieldwork, diary methods, think-aloud protocols, practice research — those specific constraints are real and varied. What the principle rules out is treating data as categorically exempt from openness because it happens to be complex, interpretive, or culturally sensitive.
CORE data, understood as material to be built upon and modified through further recontextualisation rather than simply reproduced (Adams et al., 2026), shifts the meaning of openness: rather than providing raw data for others to re-run the same analysis, sharing CORE data means making available the conditions of its production — considering its materiality, how it was gathered, evaluating its history and provenance, drawing attention to its limits, and navigating its relationships with data in other forms (manuscript and printed edition; recording and live performance; interview and published account).
Every dataset has components that are almost always shareable. Qualitative datasets, for example, can openly share: interview guides, codebooks, anonymised excerpts, demographic summaries, inter-rater reliability data, and analytical memos documenting how themes developed. These materials constitute the O, R, and E components of CORE — the organisation, recontextualisation, and explanation of the data — even when the C (collected raw material) cannot be fully released. This is often the most transferable and generative part of a dataset for AHSS research because it makes visible the interpretive work rather than just the source material.

5.4.1 A note on consent:
For any study, consent determines the flexibility you have at the point of sharing, and it must be designed before data collection, not at archiving. Consent forms that do not mention future data sharing, or only cover it negatively, close off options that are difficult to reopen. To give participants genuine choice and researchers corresponding flexibility, consent forms should distinguish between (a) anonymised quotation in publications, (b) deposit in a restricted-access archive for future research under ethical oversight, and (c) retention within the research team. Writing the consent form with data sharing in mind is not additional work, but the same work, done more carefully.


5.4.2 A note on qualitative data:
Focusing in on qualitative studies, anonymisation of data is more complex than name removal. Participants in music psychology or ethnomusicology research often describe experiences or biographical details specific enough to identify a small or distinctive community. A participant who mentions being the only professional player of a particular instrument in a named city, or whose description of a formative musical experience locates them within a distinctive subculture, may be identifiable to community members regardless of pseudonymisation. Effective anonymisation requires altering or removing contextual details and identifiers — a process that should itself be documented so readers understand what has been changed. Consulting institutional ethics committees and national data protection frameworks (UK GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018; EU GDPR) at the design stage before data collection — rather than at the archiving stage where options are already constrained — is strongly advisable.






Almost-always sharable qualitative/AHSS materials
Even when raw data cannot be released, the following typically fall on the open side of “as open as possible, as closed as necessary”:

Interview guide or protocol: the questions, prompts, or stimulus materials used
Codebook: category definitions, examples, decision rules, evolution across coding rounds
Consent form template: the wording used, so others can assess what permissions were granted
Anonymised excerpts: the quotes used in the published paper, or a representative set
Demographic summary: aggregated participant characteristics without identifying combinations
Inter-rater reliability data: agreement statistics and any adjudication notes
Analytical memos: interpretive notes documenting how themes developed (where not participant-identifiable)
Research practice reflections: accounts of how decisions were made, what changed, and why
Annotated bibliographies: the literature context into which the data is recontextualised

For restricted-access deposit of sensitive material, the UK Data Service, DANS, and OSF all support configurations that make a project publicly findable while controlling access to raw files.

title: 5  Open Data
section: 5.5 Working open data into your research workflow
text:
5.5 Working open data into your research workflow
A common objection to open data is that it creates additional work. This can be true when data sharing is treated as something done after the research is complete, rather than designed into the research process from the beginning. Preparing a dataset for release at submission — when you have moved on mentally, partially forgotten your own variable coding, and lost track of which file is the final version — would understandably be burdensome. The solution is not to push through that burden on every project, but to stop creating it.
The practical shift is clearly documenting the research process as you do it. Open data documentation is simply an explanation of all research stages and decisions made available and understandable to a third party. Noting decisions as you make them (rather than reconstructing them during writing up) is smaller work than the catch-up, better scholarship, and a prerequisite for meaningful openness. The E (Explained) component of CORE is best applied as an account of interpretive work that the research involves anyway, captured as it happens.
Documenting as you go:

Create a README file explaining dataset contents during data collection
Write and save codebook versions with definitions before analysis while you are actively deciding what your variables mean and their arrangement
Document selection criteria and organisation for archival collection in real time
Note how an interview corpus was assembled and why (e.g., inclusion criteria, collection method)
Record what scholarly debates this dataset enters and how that framing was established, before the selection and refinement stages







Minimum viable structure for a shareable dataset
A shareable dataset does not need to be elaborate. At minimum:

A README.txt at the top level: what the dataset is, what study it came from, what each file contains, any caveats about limitations or missing data, where it fits into scholarly conversation
A codebook or equivalent: defined variables/categories, decision rules (e.g., selection rationale, interpretive notes, scope of the collection)
Data in open formats: CSV for tabular data, plain text or PDF/A for documents and qualitative material, MIDI or MusicXML for symbolic music
Documentation on the analytical process and decision making
Any analysis scripts needed to reproduce reported results

Writing these in a readable manner (for others and your future self!) during the project rather than at the end is faster, more informative, and more helpful down the line.

title: 5  Open Data
text:
5.7 Original materials, stimuli, and copyright
Commercial copyright represents one of the most clearly bounded applications of “as closed as necessary” in music research. Copyright applies to the audio files themselves, which in many cases prevents researchers from redistributing commercial recordings used as stimuli. It does not apply to the stimulus list, the selection rationale, the acoustic features extracted from the files, the participant ratings collected about them, or the documentation of how they were used.
The most straightforward resolution, where the research question and purpose allow, is to use materials that can be freely shared from the outset (e.g., CC-licensed audio). Public domain recordings — performances of works whose copyright has expired under the applicable jurisdiction’s threshold — are another route, though the threshold varies and must be verified. Purpose-composed or purpose-recorded stimuli, commissioned for a study and released under a CC licence, eliminate the copyright constraint. Where openly licensed stimuli are available, and the research question does not specifically require commercially embedded music, choosing them at the design stage is the “as open as possible” decision.
Practice-based music researchers face a related but distinct version of this challenge. For a composer, performer, or sound artist whose research is the creative work, sharing the work under an open licence is a significant decision with professional implications that differ from those of sharing an experimental stimulus set. The appropriate response here is not to require full openness of the creative output itself, but to share as much of the research around the practice as possible: scores, performance instructions, methodological documentation, reflections on process, audio and video recordings of study performances, and structured dataset descriptions that make the project navigable and citable.






Case study: open research in music, drama, and performing arts
Jacobs (2022) documents a senior academic, dramaturg, choreographer, and curator whose work spans archival, curatorial, and interdisciplinary practice communities. The case study illustrates how AHSS practice researchers can engage with open research without compromising the integrity of their creative work: the work itself — live performance, collaborative creative practice — is not open-sourced, nor should it be. What is shared instead is the research around the practice: documentation of methods and know-how that enables others to build on the work; combinations of academic scholarship, archival material, and technical infrastructure; data, talks, catalogues, and essays that would otherwise be lost without openness. The case study notes that much of the value of this work to others would be inaccessible without openness, including reflexive accounts of the roles of artists and audiences that are themselves a form of analytical explanation — the E in CORE.



The Garden of Forking Paths project (McLaughlin, 2022) is a citable and interactive project that demonstrates this at scale: a practice research project in composition that shared tutorials and example videos, scores and audio for solo and duo pieces, a blog documenting “the research as it happened”, and a dataset description listing resource locations and deposit dates. The creative work itself remains the composer’s; the research around it is openly available for others to learn from, build on, and recontextualise.






Case study: The Garden of Forking Paths
Scott McLaughlin’s Garden of Forking Paths (McLaughlin, 2022) — a practice research project on material-indeterminacy in open-form composition for clarinets — illustrates what open data means for music practice research. The project made available: tutorials and example videos; writing, talks, and workshop materials; scores and audio for solo and duo pieces; a mix of studies and concert work; and a blog framed as a way to “dive into the research as it happened.” Alongside these, a dataset description was deposited listing resource locations, deposit dates, and contextual information. The creative works remain the composer’s; the research process, methodology, and materials are openly shared. This is CORE data openness: the Collected and Organised research materials around a creative practice, Recontextualised in relation to existing debates about indeterminacy and instrument design, Explained through a documented process that others can follow, critique, and build upon.
The project is archived at the University of Leeds Research Data Repository (doi: 10.5518/1117) with an accompanying project website at forkingpaths.leeds.ac.uk.



A well-documented stimulus list deposited with its own DOI is a citable research output in its own right — representing genuine curatorial and analytical work that others can query, extend, and build upon, even if they must re-acquire the files independently.
When commercial recordings are used, and the audio cannot be shared, the minimum expectation is a stimulus list detailed enough for another researcher to reconstruct or closely approximate the set. This should specify: title, artist, and album; excerpt boundaries in seconds; any normalisation procedure or audio processing applied; a persistent identifier (e.g., Spotify URI, ISRC, or equivalent). Sharing acoustic features extracted from the stimuli (tempo, mode, spectral features, dynamic range), and participant ratings collected about them, provides additional reproducible material without any copyright implications.
Notated scores and symbolic data (MIDI, MusicXML, MEI) occupy a different part of the copyright landscape as musical compositions and specific recordings are legally distinct. A MIDI transcription of a public-domain work can typically be shared freely. For contemporary works, rights-holder clarification or use of datasets with already-secured permissions is the appropriate route. The music21 corpus, RISM, and the Josquin Research Project are examples of publicly available symbolic collections with clarified permissions.






Stimulus reporting: what copyright closes, and what it does not
Copyright in a commercial recording prevents redistributing the audio file. It does not prevent sharing:

Full bibliographic details: title, artist/performer, album, recording year
Persistent identifiers: Spotify URI, ISRC, YouTube URL (supplement with bibliographic details given link rot)
Excerpt boundaries: start time (MM:SS) and duration (seconds)
Playback level and normalisation procedure (e.g. RMS normalisation to −20 dBFS)
File format and sample rate used in the experiment
Audio processing: filtering, fade-in/out, EQ
Selection rationale: what criteria governed inclusion and exclusion
Extracted acoustic features: tempo, key/mode, spectral centroid, dynamic range, etc.
Participant ratings collected on the stimuli: familiarity, valence, arousal, etc.

A stimulus documentation file deposited as a dataset with its own DOI is a citable, reusable research output — not merely a supplementary methods note.

title: 5  Open Data
text:
5.8 Summary
The governing principle for this chapter is as open as possible, as closed as necessary (UK Research and Innovation, 2016). Open is the default position, and the burden of justification falls on any departure from it. For music research, that burden is sometimes substantial — commercial copyright on audio, ethical obligations to participants, cultural sensitivities in ethnographic contexts, legal requirements under GDPR. But these are reasons to close specific elements of specific projects, not reasons to treat the field as broadly exempt from open data expectations.
Across the range of disciplines that make up music research, openness takes different forms. For MIR and computational musicology, it looks most like FAIR-compliant dataset sharing with open code. For music psychology, it includes both that quantitative infrastructure and the qualitative and mixed-methods dimensions addressed here. For musicology, ethnomusicology, music education, and practice research, the CORE framework (Adams et al., 2026; Gilby et al., 2022) provides a more fitting account: sharing the collection, organisation, recontextualisation, and explanation of research data, including outputs that do not look like “data” in a quantitative sense. These AHSS outputs are open and appropriate research contributions, not a workaround for the impossibility of full openness.
The practical work of open data is mostly front-loadable. Designed into the research from the start — through consent language, file format choices, stimulus selection, contemporaneous documentation — it costs far less than the retrospective preparation it replaces and produces better-organised research along the way. Gathering CORE data, conveying interpretations transparently, maintaining disciplinary standards, and privileging diversity, transparency, and accountability in how research is conducted and shared is “careful scholarship in its truest sense” (Gilby et al., 2022). Open data is not an additional obligation on top of good research, but is part of what good research in music looks like.






Sharing documented pieces — early decisions that matter:

Consent language: draft consent forms to include explicit data sharing permissions from the outset, distinguishing between quotation in publications, restricted-access archiving, and full public release (see Section 5.4)
File formats: choose non-proprietary open formats at the point of file creation — CSV over .xlsx for tabular data; plain text or PDF/A for documents; MIDI or MusicXML for symbolic music (see Section 5.5)
Licensing: apply a Creative Commons licence (CC-BY 4.0 recommended default) to materials you create at the point of creating them; more restrictive clauses (Noncommercial, Non-Derivative, Share Alike) are available where needed
Audio stimuli: where the research question allows, select openly licensed or purpose-recorded audio rather than commercial recordings — this decision at the design stage removes a constraint that cannot be resolved later (see Section 5.7)
Open notebooks/blogs: for practice research, a project blog or structured open notebook maintained as the research unfolds creates a time-stamped record that can be shared when the project is complete (Scroggie et al., 2023)
Repository: register a GitHub repository, OSF project, or equivalent early — this gives a persistent link for the dataset before it is complete, and creates a home for documentation as it accumulates rather than all at once at submission (see Section 5.6)

title: 6  Reproducible research
text:
6.1 What is “Reproducible research”?
Reproducibility in research typically refers to the ability to obtain the same findings given the same data, code, and methods. This is possible when researchers share their data and code alongside a publication or make these materials available upon request. The advantage of sharing them alongside the publication is that the results remain reproducible even if the original author can no longer be reached.
The concept is closely related to replicability, but with an important distinction: whereas replicability refers to repeating a study by collecting new data or conducting a new experiment, reproducibility refers to repeating the data analysis using the same data, code, and other materials as in the original study. Although these terms are sometimes used interchangeably or are defined differently across disciplines (Plesser, 2018), we follow the definitions established by the National Academies of Sciences (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2019), which have also been recently adopted by the Association for Computing Machinery (ACM):
Reproducibility and replicability do not necessarily depend on each other: a study may be reproducible if the original analysis can be rerun, but it may not be replicable if the effect is not found in a new sample. Conversely, a finding might be replicated in some other context, but it may be irreproducible if the analysis code or data of the original study is not available or has issues.

title: 6  Reproducible research
text:
6.2 Reproducibility and replication problems
While we would like all reported evidence to be reproducible, this is not always the case. Brian A. Nosek et al. (2022) identifies two possible scenarios leading to such failures. The most common is a process reproducibility failure: there is insufficient access to data, code (or the information needed to recreate the code), software, or other resources required to reproduce the results. The second type is called outcome reproducibility failure, which occurs when a reanalysis can be performed, but results obtained differ from those originally reported. Outcome reproducibility failures may arise from issues in either the original study or the reproduction attempt.
Process reproducibility failure is rather typical among academia. A clear example of this relates to data sharing practices (see Chapter 5): many researchers choose to withdraw their submissions during the review process rather than make the associated datasets publicly available upon editorial request (Miyakawa, 2020), either due to knowledge barriers on data and code archival, data reuse concerns, or lack of career incentives (Gomes et al., 2022).
Reproducibility problems can make replication (see Chapter 7) particularly difficult because, in order to repeat a study (e.g., with a different sample of participants), it is important to know exactly what was done in the original research. Reproducibility was generally much harder in the past, especially before modern software tooling: before the 1980s, calculations were often performed manually, and data was stored and shared on paper. After the personal computer revolution, and particularly before the widespread adoption of the internet, code was increasingly used but was often not shared, and computational environments were more difficult to recreate (Peng & Hicks, 2021). Nowadays, version control systems, cloud storage, workflow management tools and public repositories greatly facilitate research reproducibility. However, despite these advances, reproducibility problems remain an important challenge in psychological research.
Replication problems are currently a major concern, as many previously published findings have been difficult to replicate, owing to factors such as underpowered studies, differences in participants, contexts, and procedures across studies investigating the same phenomenon, and publication bias (Stanley et al., 2018). In response to these challenges, various solutions have been proposed, ranging from the registered report format, where researchers submit the hypotheses and methods for peer review before collecting data (Obels et al., 2020), to more stringent statistical standards for the psychological sciences (Johnson et al., 2017).






Reproducibility and Replicability 
This framing also clarifies an important distinction between two related but conceptually separate concepts: reproducibility and replicability (Brian A. Nosek & Errington, 2020). Reproducibility refers to the ability to obtain the same analytical results from the same data using the same code and procedures. A failure of reproducibility—for example, when a reported analysis cannot be reproduced from the shared dataset—indicates a problem with the analysis or reporting rather than with the underlying empirical claim. Replicability, by contrast, refers to whether a new study, conducted with a fresh sample and potentially varying some procedural details, arrives at a similar conclusion. Failures of reproducibility and failures of replicability are distinct problems that call for different solutions.
In music research, both forms of transparency matter. Reproducible research requires sharing data, analysis code, and sufficient procedural detail for others to verify the reported results (see Chapter 5). Replicable research requires that original findings be robust enough to emerge in new samples and contexts, and that procedures are reported with enough specificity for others to implement them. A study that uses commercially licensed music recordings, withholds participant-level data, or describes stimuli only vaguely poses challenges for both reproducibility and replication—challenges that open materials practices are designed to address.



Psychological research faces several factors that may increase the risk of false findings, including the complexity of human behaviour, the testing of multiple variables and hypotheses (see Chapter 9), and the use of relatively small sample sizes in many studies involving human participants. Furthermore, much of the research published in leading psychology journals is based on WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) populations, which are outliers on many measurable psychological dimensions compared with populations worldwide (Henrich et al., 2010a, 2010b).

title: 6  Reproducible research
text:
6.3 Reproducible music research
While music psychology has made some progress in recognizing these problems (Eerola, 2024; Frieler et al., 2013) and promoting research transparency, it is clear that many studies still do not adopt practices that allow other scientists to easily verify and reproduce their analyses. Eerola (2024) examined research articles from five music psychology journals and found that only 5% included data availability statements and just 1% provided data analysis scripts.

In recent years, researchers in music-related fields have published fully reproducible workflows in which the entire research pipeline can be recreated, from raw data processing to final manuscript (e.g., Eerola, 2024; Bertolo et al., 2025; Cho et al., 2025).

title: 6  Reproducible research
section: 6.4 Reproducible research in the AI era
text:
6.4 Reproducible research in the AI era
Large language models (LLMs) are arguably a double-edged sword with regard to research reproducibility. One reason is that AI training by large companies lacks transparency (Kuru, 2024; Kwon, 2025), making researchers (and the broader public) increasingly cautious about what is shared online. A further concern is that LLMs are functionally stochastic, and that feeding input data into them can produce inconsistent results, leading to process reproducibility failure, although this concern remains debated across fields (Vangala et al., 2026; Windisch et al., 2026). Additionally, researchers may rely on LLMs for everyday data analyses (e.g., computing exploratory correlations) but may not retrieve the code used by the LLMs, whether by choice or because it may be impossible; also certain AI models may become unavailable over time, resulting in a lack of traceability.
On the other hand, LLMs can greatly facilitate research reproduction tasks, and numerous benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate the quality of an AI agent’s attempt to replicate or reproduce existing studies (Bhaskar & Stodden, 2024; Nguyen et al., 2026). Recent recommendations for ensuring reproducibility in LLM-assisted scientific analysis pipelines include obtaining results through LLM-generated code rather than directly from LLMs, verifing and reporting LLM-generated results, preferring open-weight LLMs, documenting the model and version used, and ensuring consistency of results across multiple runs and models (Dunn et al., 2026).

title: 6  Reproducible research
text:
6.5 Workflow
A crucial challenge in reproducible research is how to create a well documented and straightforward set of instructions that would allow other researchers to independently reproduce study results (Antunes & Hill, 2024). One approach to addressing this problem is literate programming (Knuth, 1984), which essentially consists of creating documents containing explanations of procedures or algorithms interleaved with source code snippets embedded within the text. Let’s for instance take the MIRtoolbox, an open source MATLAB toolbox for musical feature extraction from audio:






NoteLiterate programming example



To estimate the global tempo of the musical recording using MIRtoolbox, we first import it as an audio object using miraudio and then compute its tempo via mirtempo:
s = miraudio('my_song.wav');
t = mirtempo(s);
The variable t will contain the estimated tempo, expressed in beats per minute (BPM).


As a side note on this example, MATLAB is a proprietary language, but the MIRtoolbox is openly available. While the tempo estimation algorithms of MIRToolbox (mirtempo), librosa (tempo), and Essentia (TempoCNN) are open source, numerous studies have been conducted using closed source algorithms for estimating tempo and other musical features (e.g., Spotify Web API). Proprietary cloud algorithms are, however, problematic for replication, since providers may modify or retrain them over time.
A modern realization of the literate programming idea is provided by interactive notebooks, which allow not only the presentation of neatly formatted code and text cells, but also the execution of code. Project Jupyter is one of the most widely used interactive notebook environments and has grown rapidly from its initial focus on the Julia, Python, and R languages to supporting over 100 programming languages through its kernel ecosystem. Cloud-based environments based on Jupyter, such as Google Colab and JupyterHub, further simplify setup and workflows by executing code remotely, meaning that computations are carried out on remote servers rather than on a local machine. This makes it possible to create interactive online resources for teaching, such as online textbooks on audio analysis (Ali, 2025) and music processing (Müller, 2015).
Beyond interactive notebooks, more complex endeavors require a clear project structure, including, for example, a README file, a file specifying software dependencies, and subfolders for data, code, results, and the manuscript itself. There are also dedicated libraries that can be used to create a standardized directory structure and template files for reproducible research, such as rrtools for R and DrWatson for Julia. In fully reproducible research workflows, all analyses, including the creation of tables and figures, are regenerated, and in some cases even the entire manuscript is compiled using tools such as Quarto or R Markdown. Cloud-based platforms for sharing, running, and reproducing code, such as Code Ocean, have been used to ensure that the published results can be recreated by others. Other relevant cloud services facilitating the reproducibility of research workflows include Renku and Whole Tale.
Because code, analysis decisions, and manuscript content are subject to change over the course of a research process (and since it may be necessary to go back and forth between different versions of a pipeline), version control can greatly facilitate these workflows. Git is currently the most widely used version control system, and GitHub is a popular Git hosting service that supports collaborative software development. Version control can also be used to manage the versions of the software and libraries used in an analysis. This is particularly important when working with programming languages such as Python, R, or Julia, where changes in package versions can affect the results of an analysis. Using virtual environments to specify and record the exact versions of software dependencies makes it easier for other researchers to recreate the same computational setup at a later point in time. Such practices can therefore contribute to the reproducibility of computational research by ensuring that not only the code, but also the software environment in which it was executed, can be restored. Examples include Conda), a package manager and environment management system. Using this software, multiple environments with different software versions and dependencies can coexist on the same computer without interfering with each other.

title: 6  Reproducible research
text:
6.6 Conclusions
Music research can greatly benefit from reproducible practices, given the diversity of methods and data involved in studying music perception, cognition, emotions, behaviour, performance, and social and cultural contexts. Scientific work should provide a practical path for others to re-run analyses and verify the results obtained. This requires maximizing transparency throughout the analysis process, developing software implementations that are easy to re-execute, and ensuring that computations produce consistent results across multiple runs (Krafczyk et al., 2021). While achieving full reproducibility is not always straightforward or ever possible, researchers today have access to excellent tools and resources that can facilitate the verification and reuse of research results. Reproducibility can make existing knowledge reusable (e.g. in meta-analyses, follow-up studies, and teaching), and ultimately increase credibility and contribute to the advancement of research.
